name: The Missing Fundamental
statement: Remove the bass note itself and the ear still hears its pitch, inferred from the overtones.
statementAccent: the ear still hears its pitch, inferred from the overtones
meaning: The missing fundamental is an auditory phenomenon in which a listener perceives the pitch of a fundamental frequency even when that frequency is physically absent from the sound and only its higher harmonics are present. If a tone contains components at, say, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, and five hundred hertz, the harmonics of a hundred-hertz fundamental, but not the hundred-hertz component itself, the perceived pitch is still that of the missing hundred-hertz note. The brain infers the fundamental from the regular spacing of the harmonics rather than reading it off directly from energy at that frequency. Also called virtual pitch, residue pitch, or periodicity pitch, the phenomenon demonstrates that pitch is a perceptual construction, not simply the lowest frequency present in a sound. It has profound practical consequences, most familiarly in explaining how small loudspeakers, earbuds, and telephones convey the pitch of bass notes they cannot physically reproduce, because the ear reconstructs the fundamental from the overtones they do transmit.
mechanism: Pitch perception depends on the pattern and periodicity of a sound's harmonics, not merely on the presence of a component at the fundamental frequency. When harmonics are spaced by a common interval, the greatest common divisor of their frequencies, the auditory system detects that periodicity and assigns a pitch corresponding to it, even if no energy exists at that frequency. Two families of theory explain how: pattern-recognition accounts hold that the brain matches the set of present harmonics to the harmonic template of a fundamental and reports that fundamental; temporal accounts hold that the pitch is extracted from the repetition period of the combined waveform, encoded in the timing of neural firing in the auditory nerve. Both capture the key point that the hundred-hertz periodicity of a sound built from its higher harmonics is preserved even without the hundred-hertz component, so the ear hears a hundred-hertz pitch. The phenomenon was studied through a long nineteenth- and twentieth-century debate, from Seebeck and Ohm to Helmholtz and later Schouten, whose residue theory established that the effect is not merely a distortion product generated in the ear.

examples.text: A tone of two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, and five hundred hertz, harmonics of a hundred, is heard at the pitch of the absent hundred-hertz fundamental.
Phones cannot pass frequencies below about three hundred hertz, yet a male voice with a lower fundamental is heard at its true pitch, reconstructed from harmonics.
Tiny drivers that cannot emit deep bass synthesize the upper harmonics, and the ear supplies the missing low pitch.

variants.name: Pattern recognition
variants.text: The account that the brain matches the present harmonics to a fundamental's harmonic template and reports that fundamental's pitch.

variants.name: Periodicity or temporal theory
variants.text: The account that pitch is read from the repetition period of the waveform, encoded in the timing of auditory-nerve firing.

whyItMatters: The missing fundamental is a cornerstone demonstration in psychoacoustics that pitch is constructed by the brain rather than simply detected. By showing that the ear reports a pitch with no physical energy at that frequency, it overturned the naive idea that pitch equals the lowest frequency present and forced theories of hearing to account for periodicity and pattern, shaping the modern understanding of how the auditory system extracts pitch. Its practical reach is enormous: it explains how telephones, small radios, laptop speakers, and earbuds convey the pitch of bass notes and low voices they cannot physically reproduce, a fact exploited deliberately by audio engineers who synthesize upper harmonics to give small devices apparent bass. The phenomenon also illuminates music perception, since the perceived pitch of complex instrumental tones follows their harmonic structure.

working.text: present a complex tone containing the higher harmonics of a fundamental but not the fundamental frequency itself.
let the auditory system read the common spacing of the harmonics, the periodicity that corresponds to the fundamental.
perceive the pitch of the missing fundamental, reconstructed from the pattern of overtones.

limits: The missing fundamental is a robust perceptual phenomenon, but the precise mechanism, whether pattern recognition, temporal periodicity, or a combination, remains a matter of theory and research, so the effect is better established than its full explanation. The clarity and strength of the perceived pitch depend on which harmonics are present, their number, and their loudness, and the effect can weaken when only very high harmonics remain. Historically it was long confused with nonlinear distortion products, difference tones generated in the ear, until Schouten's work showed the pitch survives even when such products are masked. The naming of the pitch it produces, virtual, residue, or periodicity pitch, varies across the literature. So the missing fundamental reliably shows that pitch is inferred from harmonic structure rather than read from the fundamental, while the detailed account of how the brain does so is still refined.
misreadings: The perceived pitch is not evidence that the fundamental is secretly present; it is genuinely absent, and the ear infers its pitch from the spacing of the harmonics. The effect is not merely a distortion tone produced in the ear, since it persists when such products are masked. And it shows that pitch is not simply the lowest frequency in a sound, so treating the heard bass note as physically present, or the phenomenon as ear distortion, misreads an illusion that reveals pitch to be a construction from the pattern of overtones.
origin: A psychoacoustic phenomenon studied through a long nineteenth- and twentieth-century debate from Seebeck and Ohm to Helmholtz and J. F. Schouten, whose residue theory established that the pitch is inferred from harmonic periodicity rather than a distortion product.
